newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam nudges currency lower to tackle trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam nudges currency lower to tackle trade gap.

text.p: Vietnam's central bank has again lowered its official peg for the local currency against the dollar in a bid to narrow the country's yawning trade gap by gradual devaluation, foreign exchange traders said on Wednesday.
They said the State Bank of Vietnam had cut its official pivot rate for the dong to 11,065 per dollar from 11,060 at the start of the week as corporate demand for the U.S. currency remained strong.
Commercial banks may buy and sell at rates up to one percent either side of the pivot, which means the official trading band now has 10,955 as its ceiling and 11,175 as its lower limit.
The dong was trading just short of its new floor in light trade on the interbank market on Wednesday, which put its decline over the past six weeks at more than 0.8 percent.
"Everyone is hanging on to dollars, it's not a two-way street," said one trader at a foreign bank in Ho Chi Minh City.
He reckoned that the central bank would probably continue to lower its official peg, by an average of about two dong per day, in the run-up to the lunar New Year holiday early next month.

Bankers say the depreciation policy is aimed at making imports more expensive and exports cheaper to bridge a rapidly widening trade gap. The trade deficit leapt to a record $4.0 billion in 1996, equivalent to about 18 percent of annual gross domestic product (GDP).

The dong's stability at around 11,000 since 1994, combined with high inflation, had led to a real appreciation of about 10 percent against the currencies of Vietnam's main trading partners by mid-1996.
Although divided over how effective a depreciation would be in tackling the trade deficit, analysts agree that the authorities are right not to allow a rapid slide in the currency's value.
Public trust in the nascent banking system remains very low and many people still prefer to stash dollar bills or gold bars under a mattress at home than open a dong deposit account.
David Hutcheson, Hongkong Bank's chief executive in Vietnam, said the depreciation could sharpen the competitive edge of agricultural products, on which Vietnam is heavily dependent.

However, he said the authorities should not try to look for more than a five or six percent depreciation over one year because they needed to encourage confidence in the dong and whittle away at the dollar's role in Vietnam as a parallel currency.
